lede: Some quantities need a direction as well as a size. Walk 400 m out and 100 m back and you have covered 500 m, yet you finish only 300 m from the start. This Higher-tier topic separates distance from displacement and speed from velocity, then builds acceleration, and retardation, from velocity.
can: Sort motion quantities into vectors and scalars, and pair each vector with its scalar
Calculate average velocity from a displacement, and acceleration from a change in velocity
Rearrange a = (v − u) ÷ t for a final velocity, and describe a negative acceleration as retardation

md: Swim two lengths of a 25 m pool and you have swum 50 m, yet you finish exactly where you dived in. Both facts are true, because they describe two different quantities. Physics keeps them apart with one extra piece of information: a **direction**.

text: 1. Size only, or size and direction

md:
A **scalar** has a size only. A **vector** has a size **and a direction**.
Each motion quantity comes in a pair, one of each kind, and the two share a unit. Force and weight are vectors too; mass, time and energy are scalars.

prompt: Which of these quantities is a vector?
explain: Displacement: how far, and in which direction, from the start. Distance and speed are sizes only.

md:
**Displacement** is how far you finish from the start, in a stated direction: one straight arrow. On the walk, the distance is 500 m but the displacement is 300 m east.
Velocity comes from displacement as speed comes from distance:
**average velocity = displacement ÷ time**; in symbols, v = d ÷ t with d the displacement.
Over 250 s the walk's average speed is 2 m/s, but its average velocity is 1.2 m/s east.

title: GCSE Physics - Speed, Velocity, Distance & Displacement | Scalar & Vector Quantities
why: Six minutes that set speed beside velocity and distance beside displacement, as this section does.

prompt: A runner goes 60 m east along a straight track, then 20 m back west, taking 20 s in all. What is the size of her average velocity, in m/s?
explain: Displacement 60 − 20 = 40 m east, so the average velocity is 40 ÷ 20 = 2 m/s east. Her average speed, from the 80 m she ran, is 4 m/s.

md:
Along a straight line there are only two directions, so a sign can carry the direction. Choose one direction as **positive**; the other is then **negative**.
With east positive, 15 m/s west is a velocity of **−15 m/s**. The speed is still 15 m/s: a speed never has a sign.

title: Why bother with a sign?
md: It is the shortest way to write a direction: the one character in −15 m/s does the work of the word west. The same sign will tell you, in the next section, when something is slowing down.

prompt: East is taken as positive. A cyclist rides due west at 6 m/s. What is her velocity, in m/s?
explain: −6 m/s: the size is her speed, and the minus sign says west.

md:
**Acceleration** is the change in velocity each second: **a = (v − u) ÷ t**, with u the initial velocity, v the final velocity and t the time taken. Its unit is **m/s²**. Always final minus initial.
**Worked example.** A train slows steadily from 24 m/s to 6 m/s in 12 s.
a = (6 − 24) ÷ 12 = **−1.5 m/s²**
The minus sign says it is slowing. A negative acceleration is a **retardation**: here, a retardation of 1.5 m/s². Many videos say **deceleration**; either earns the mark.

prompt: A car slows steadily from 20 m/s to 8 m/s in 4 s. What is its acceleration, in m/s²?
explain: (8 − 20) ÷ 4 = −3 m/s², a retardation of 3 m/s². A bare 3 would say the car was speeding up.

alt: A bar for a starting velocity of 4 metres per second joined to a dashed bar for the 3 metres per second gained at 0.5 metres per second squared for 6 seconds, making 7 metres per second.

md: Rearranged, the same equation gives the final velocity: **v = u + a × t**. Multiply the acceleration by the time to get the velocity gained, then add the velocity it started with: 4 + 0.5 × 6 = 7 m/s.

title: The step most candidates missed
md: In the March 2026 Higher paper most candidates found an acceleration correctly, but few then used a = (v − u) ÷ t to reach a final velocity. Write the equation, put in the three values you know, and solve for v.

md: When the velocity changes steadily, its average is halfway: **average velocity = (initial velocity + final velocity) ÷ 2**. Multiply by the time to get the displacement. Using the final velocity alone assumes it was reached at the very start, and gives an answer that is too big.

prompt: A skater's velocity rises steadily from 2 m/s to 8 m/s in 4 s. What is her displacement in that time, in metres?

md:
Say which quantities are vectors (size and direction) and which are scalars (size only), and pair them.
Tell distance from displacement and speed from velocity, and find average velocity = displacement ÷ time.
Use a sign for direction along a line, with one direction chosen as positive.
Calculate a = (v − u) ÷ t and call a negative acceleration a retardation.
Rearrange for a final velocity, and use the average of two velocities for a displacement.

This topic is Higher tier only. Expect a scalar-or-vector sort worth [1] each, then calculations worth [3] or [4]: the equation, the substitution and the answer, with a mark for the minus sign when something slows. The first mark is the equation; the last is the value with its sign. Stuck? Write a = (v − u) ÷ t, fill in the three values you know, and solve for the fourth.
